Graph binomial coefficients and a positivity conjecture
of Guo and KrattenthalerThanks: Corresponding author: Daniel Yaqubi

Madjid Mirzavaziri Address: Department of Pure Mathematics, Ferdowsi University of Mashhad, Mashhad, Iran Email address: mirzavaziri@um.ac.ir, mirzavaziri@gmail.com and Daniel Yaqubi Address: Department of Computer Science, University of Torbat-e Jam, Torbat-e Jam, Iran Email address: yaqubi@tjamcaas.ac.ir, daniel_yaqubi@yahoo.es
Abstract.

We investigate Conjecture 7.4 of Guo and Krattenthaler [4], which predicts that for every positive integer nn, the polynomial

Pn​(q)=(1−q)2(1−q10​n−1)​(1−q15​n−1)​[30​n5​n]qP_{n}(q)=\frac{(1-q)^{2}}{(1-q^{10n-1})(1-q^{15n-1})}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{30n}{5n}_{q}

has non-negative coefficients, except for q1q^{1} and q125​n2−25​n+3q^{125n^{2}-25n+3}, which equal −1-1. We study this problem through three main perspectives: First, by linking the boundary coefficients to the second differences of the partition function, we settle the first and last 25​n+125n+1 coefficients via a novel partition injection. Second, by introducing a “defect” generalization of Andrews’ classical lemma, we reduce the conjecture to an almost-unimodality property and employ a uniform saddle-point analysis to prove it analytically for all large n≥2⋅1029n\geq 2\cdot 10^{29}. Finally, we connect these quotients to graph binomial coefficients, providing a natural orbit-counting interpretation via Burnside’s lemma on directed cycles and paths.

Key words and phrases: 
qq-binomial coefficient, Gaussian polynomial, positivity, unimodality, graph binomial coefficient, Burnside’s lemma, cyclic sieving, partition function
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
05A10, 05A17, 05A30, 05C30, 11B65

1. Introduction

Let [n]q=1+q+⋯+qn−1[n]_{q}=1+q+\dots+q^{n-1} denote the qq-integer, and let

[Nk]q=(1−qN)(1−qN−1)⋯(1−qN−k+1)(1−qk)(1−qk−1)⋯(1−q)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{N}{k}_{q}=\frac{(1-q^{N})(1-q^{N-1})\cdots(1-q^{N-k+1})}{(1-q^{k})(1-q^{k-1})\cdots(1-q)}

be the Gaussian polynomial (qq-binomial coefficient). It is a classical result that [Nk]q\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{N}{k}_{q} is a reciprocal and unimodal polynomial with non-negative integer coefficients, serving as the generating function for kk-element subsets S⊆{0,1,…,N−1}S\subseteq\{0,1,\dots,N-1\} weighted by

w⁡(S)=∑s∈Ss−(k2).w(S)=\sum_{s\in S}s-\binom{k}{2}.

In [4], Guo and Krattenthaler established several remarkable divisibility properties for binomial coefficients by lifting them to the qq-setting. A representative result [4, Theorem 3.1] asserts that the rational function

(1−q)2(1−q10​n−1)​(1−q15​n−1)​[30​n5​n]q\frac{(1-q)^{2}}{(1-q^{10n-1})(1-q^{15n-1})}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{30n}{5n}_{q}

is a polynomial in qq, implying the divisibility relation (10​n−1)​(15​n−1)|(30​n5​n)(10n-1)(15n-1)\mid\binom{30n}{5n}. Among the four conjectures proposed in [4, Section 7] with Conjectures 7.2 and 7.3 now settled [8] the remaining positivity problem, Conjecture 7.4, stands as a central open question in the study of qq-binomial quotients (see also [9, 10, 11]). It predicts the following precise coefficient-sign pattern:

Conjecture 1.1 ([4, Conjecture 7.4]).

For all positive integers nn and all 0≤k≤125​n2−25​n+40\leq k\leq 125n^{2}-25n+4, the coefficient of qkq^{k} in the polynomial

Pn​(q)=(1−q)2(1−q10​n−1)​(1−q15​n−1)​[30​n5​n]qP_{n}(q)=\frac{(1-q)^{2}}{(1-q^{10n-1})(1-q^{15n-1})}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{30n}{5n}_{q}

is non-negative, except for k=1k=1 and k=125​n2−25​n+3k=125n^{2}-25n+3, where the coefficient equals −1-1.

The original positivity proofs in [4] rely on a classical reduction lemma by Andrews [1], which inherently requires unimodality. However, Conjecture 1.1 lies beyond its scope: although dividing [30​n5​n]q\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{30n}{5n}_{q} by [10​n−1]q[10n-1]_{q} yields a non-negative intermediate polynomial, this polynomial fails to be unimodal (its coefficients begin as 1,0,1,…1,0,1,\dots). Consequently, Andrews’ lemma cannot be applied iteratively to clear the second factor, necessitating new analytical and combinatorial tools.

The primary objective of this paper is to solve Conjecture 1.1 through a unified framework. First, we link the initial coefficients of Pn​(q)P_{n}(q) to the second differences of the partition function Δ2​p​(t)\Delta^{2}p(t), allowing us to settle the boundary coefficients via partition monotonicity. To bypass the failure of Andrews’ lemma under non-unimodality, we generalize the lemma to allow a controlled defect, reducing the conjecture to the almost-unimodality of a single qq-quotient.

For large-scale behavior, we deploy a uniform saddle-point analysis on a double contour integral representation to prove asymptotic positivity, solving Conjecture 1.1 for all n≥2⋅1029n\geq 2\cdot 10^{29} and thereby reducing the problem to a finite computational range. Finally, we extend the quotient family to general parameters mm and provide a combinatorial interpretation using graph binomial coefficients and Burnside’s orbit-counting lemma.

Throughout this paper, for a polynomial or formal power series f⁡(q)f(q), we write [qt]​f​(q)[q^{t}]f(q) for the coefficient of qtq^{t}, and write f⁡(q)≥0f(q)\geq 0 to indicate that all coefficients of f⁡(q)f(q) are non-negative.

2. Polynomiality for the whole family

For m≥1m\geq 1, let a=2​m−1a=2m-1, b=3​m−1b=3m-1, and define

Gm​(q)=[6​mm]q,P(m)​(q)=Gm​(q)[a]q​[b]q=(1−q)2(1−q2​m−1)​(1−q3​m−1)​[6​mm]q.G_{m}(q)=\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{6m}{m}_{q},\qquad P^{(m)}(q)=\frac{G_{m}(q)}{[a]_{q}[b]_{q}}=\frac{(1-q)^{2}}{(1-q^{2m-1})(1-q^{3m-1})}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{6m}{m}_{q}.
Proposition 2.1.

P(m)​(q)P^{(m)}(q) is a polynomial if and only if m≢2,3(mod5)m\not\equiv 2,3\pmod{5}. In that case, P(m)P^{(m)} is a reciprocal polynomial of degree Dm=5​m2−5​m+4D_{m}=5m^{2}-5m+4.

Proof.

We follow the cyclotomic argument of [4, proof of Theorem 3.1]. Writing qn−1=∏d|nΦd​(q)q^{n}-1=\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_{d}(q), we express P(m)​(q)=∏d≥2Φd​(q)edP^{(m)}(q)=\prod_{d\geq 2}\Phi_{d}(q)^{e_{d}} with

ed=−χ⁡(d∣2​m−1)−χ⁡(d∣3​m−1)+⌊6​md⌋−⌊md⌋−⌊5​md⌋.e_{d}=-\chi(d\mid 2m-1)-\chi(d\mid 3m-1)+\Big\lfloor\frac{6m}{d}\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\frac{m}{d}\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\frac{5m}{d}\Big\rfloor.

Since (3​m−1)−(2​m−1)=m(3m-1)-(2m-1)=m and gcd⁡(2​m−1,m)=1\gcd(2m-1,m)=1, the numbers 2​m−12m-1 and 3​m−13m-1 are coprime, ensuring that at most one of the two indicator functions is non-zero. Writing m=Q​d+xm=Qd+x with 0≤x<d0\leq x<d and X=x/dX=x/d, we have ⌊6​m/d⌋−⌊m/d⌋−⌊5​m/d⌋=⌊6​X⌋−⌊5​X⌋≥0\lfloor 6m/d\rfloor-\lfloor m/d\rfloor-\lfloor 5m/d\rfloor=\lfloor 6X\rfloor-\lfloor 5X\rfloor\geq 0. Thus, only the cases d|2​m−1d\mid 2m-1 and d|3​m−1d\mid 3m-1 require detailed attention.

If d|2​m−1d\mid 2m-1, then d|2​x−1d\mid 2x-1. Since −1≤2​x−1<2​d-1\leq 2x-1<2d, we must have 2​x−1=d2x-1=d, which implies that dd is odd and X=d+12​dX=\frac{d+1}{2d}. Consequently,

⌊6​X⌋−⌊5​X⌋=3+⌊3d⌋−⌊52+52​d⌋,\lfloor 6X\rfloor-\lfloor 5X\rfloor=3+\Big\lfloor\frac{3}{d}\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\frac{5}{2}+\frac{5}{2d}\Big\rfloor,

which equals 11 for d=3d=3 and all odd d≥7d\geq 7, and equals 00 for d=5d=5.

If d|3​m−1d\mid 3m-1, then 3​x−1∈{d,2​d}3x-1\in\{d,2d\}. If 3​x−1=d3x-1=d, then X=d+13​dX=\frac{d+1}{3d} and ⌊6​X⌋−⌊5​X⌋=2+⌊2/d⌋−⌊5/3+5/(3​d)⌋\lfloor 6X\rfloor-\lfloor 5X\rfloor=2+\lfloor 2/d\rfloor-\lfloor 5/3+5/(3d)\rfloor; this evaluates to 11 for d=2d=2 and d≥7d\geq 7, 00 for d=5d=5, while d=4d=4 is impossible. If 3​x−1=2​d3x-1=2d, then X=2​d+13​dX=\frac{2d+1}{3d} and ⌊6​X⌋−⌊5​X⌋=4+⌊2/d⌋−⌊10/3+5/(3​d)⌋=1\lfloor 6X\rfloor-\lfloor 5X\rfloor=4+\lfloor 2/d\rfloor-\lfloor 10/3+5/(3d)\rfloor=1 for every admissible dd (d≡1(mod3)d\equiv 1\pmod{3}).

Hence, ed≥0e_{d}\geq 0 for all dd, except when d=5d=5 and 5|2​m−15\mid 2m-1 or 5|3​m−15\mid 3m-1, i.e., m≡3m\equiv 3 or m≡2(mod5)m\equiv 2\pmod{5}, in which case e5=−1e_{5}=-1. The degree is given by 5​m2+2−(2​m−1)−(3​m−1)=5​m2−5​m+45m^{2}+2-(2m-1)-(3m-1)=5m^{2}-5m+4, and reciprocity follows from the reciprocal properties of GmG_{m}, [a]q[a]_{q}, and [b]q[b]_{q}. ∎

For m=5​nm=5n, we obtain D5​n=125​n2−25​n+4D_{5n}=125n^{2}-25n+4, which matches the range specified in Conjecture 1.1.

3. The exceptional coefficients and the partition function

Let p⁡(t)p(t) denote the number of partitions of tt (with p⁡(t)=0p(t)=0 for t<0t<0), and let Δ2​p​(t)=p⁡(t)−2​p​(t−1)+p⁡(t−2)\Delta^{2}p(t)=p(t)-2p(t-1)+p(t-2).

Proposition 3.1.

Let m≥2m\geq 2 with m≢2,3(mod5)m\not\equiv 2,3\pmod{5}. For 0≤t≤m0\leq t\leq m we have

[qt]​P(m)​(q)=Δ2​p​(t).[q^{t}]P^{(m)}(q)=\Delta^{2}p(t).

Moreover, Δ2​p​(0)=1\Delta^{2}p(0)=1, Δ2​p​(1)=−1\Delta^{2}p(1)=-1, and Δ2​p​(t)≥0\Delta^{2}p(t)\geq 0 for all t≥2t\geq 2. In particular, the coefficients of q0,…,qmq^{0},\dots,q^{m} in P(m)P^{(m)} are non-negative except for the coefficient −1-1 of q1q^{1}.

Proof.

The coefficient of qtq^{t} in [6​mm]q\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{6m}{m}_{q} is the number of partitions of tt with at most mm parts, each part at most 5​m5m. For t≤mt\leq m these restrictions are void, so [qt]​Gm=p⁡(t)[q^{t}]G_{m}=p(t). Since a=2​m−1>ma=2m-1>m, we have

(1−q)2(1−qa)​(1−qb)≡(1−q)2(modqm+1),\frac{(1-q)^{2}}{(1-q^{a})(1-q^{b})}\equiv(1-q)^{2}\pmod{q^{m+1}},

and the first claim follows.

For the second claim, note that p⁡(t)−p⁡(t−1)=p1′​(t)p(t)-p(t-1)=p_{1}^{\prime}(t) is the number of partitions of tt with no part equal to 11 (obtained by removing one part 11). Hence Δ2​p​(t)=p1′​(t)−p1′​(t−1)\Delta^{2}p(t)=p^{\prime}_{1}(t)-p^{\prime}_{1}(t-1). We have p1′​(0)=1p^{\prime}_{1}(0)=1, p1′​(1)=0p^{\prime}_{1}(1)=0, p1′​(2)=1p^{\prime}_{1}(2)=1, which gives the values at t=0,1,2t=0,1,2. For t≥3t\geq 3, adding 11 to the largest part maps partitions of t−1t-1 without parts 11 injectively into partitions of tt without parts 11. Hence p1′​(t)≥p1′​(t−1)p^{\prime}_{1}(t)\geq p^{\prime}_{1}(t-1). ∎

Thus, the coefficient −1-1 of q1q^{1} has a transparent origin: in the injection above, the empty partition of 00 has no image. By reciprocity, the coefficient of qDm−1q^{D_{m}-1} is also −1-1. Conjecture 1.1 can therefore be read as a boxed analogue of the inequality Δ2​p​(t)≥0\Delta^{2}p(t)\geq 0 (t≥2t\geq 2), in which the box is m×5​mm\times 5m and the factor (1−q)2(1-q)^{2} is replaced by (1−q)2/((1−q2​m−1)​(1−q3​m−1))(1-q)^{2}/((1-q^{2m-1})(1-q^{3m-1})).

3.1. The unboxed conjecture and the first 5​m5m coefficients

We now extend Proposition 3.1 from t≤mt\leq m to t≤5​mt\leq 5m. For t≤5​mt\leq 5m the bound 5​m5m on the size of the parts is void, but the bound mm on the number of parts is not. Instead of p⁡(t)p(t) we must therefore use partitions with at most mm parts. By conjugation, these are the partitions with parts at most mm. The relevant inequality is the following.

For k≥2k\geq 2, let hk​(n)h_{k}(n) be the number of partitions of nn into parts from {2,3,…,k}\{2,3,\dots,k\} (with hk​(n)=0h_{k}(n)=0 for n<0n<0), and put dk​(n)=hk​(n)−hk​(n−1)d_{k}(n)=h_{k}(n)-h_{k}(n-1). Then

(1) ∑n≥0dk​(n)​qn=1−q(1−q2)(1−q3)⋯(1−qk)=(1−q)2(q,q)k,\sum_{n\geq 0}d_{k}(n)q^{n}=\frac{1-q}{(1-q^{2})(1-q^{3})\cdots(1-q^{k})}=\frac{(1-q)^{2}}{(q;q)_{k}},

where (q;q)k=(1−q)(1−q2)⋯(1−qk)(q;q)_{k}=(1-q)(1-q^{2})\cdots(1-q^{k}). For k≥7k\geq 7 the first values are

(dk​(0),…,dk​(7))=(1,−1,1,0,1,0,2,0).(d_{k}(0),\dots,d_{k}(7))=(1,-1,1,0,1,0,2,0).
Lemma 3.2.

Let k≥9k\geq 9. Then hk​(n)≥hk​(n−1)h_{k}(n)\geq h_{k}(n-1) for every n≥2n\geq 2, and hk​(n)>hk​(n−1)h_{k}(n)>h_{k}(n-1) for every n≥8n\geq 8. In other words, dk​(n)≥0d_{k}(n)\geq 0 for n≥2n\geq 2 and dk​(n)≥1d_{k}(n)\geq 1 for n≥8n\geq 8.

Proof.

Let 𝒫⁡(n)\mathcal{P}(n) denote the set of partitions of nn into parts from {2,…,k}\{2,\dots,k\}. We define a map ι:𝒫⁡(n−1)→𝒫⁡(n)\iota\colon\mathcal{P}(n-1)\to\mathcal{P}(n). Let λ∈𝒫⁡(n−1)\lambda\in\mathcal{P}(n-1).

  1. (1)

    If λ\lambda has a part 22, replace one part 22 by 33.

Otherwise, let rr be the number of parts 33 in λ\lambda, and let ν\nu be λ\lambda with all parts 33 removed; so ν\nu has all its parts in {4,…,k}\{4,\dots,k\}.

  1. (2a)

    If rr is odd, let ι⁡(λ)=ν∪2(3​r+1)/2\iota(\lambda)=\nu\cup 2^{(3r+1)/2}.

  2. (2b)

    If r≥2r\geq 2 is even, let ι⁡(λ)=ν∪5∪2(3​r−4)/2\iota(\lambda)=\nu\cup 5\cup 2^{(3r-4)/2}.

  3. (2c)

    If r=0r=0 and the largest part λ1\lambda_{1} satisfies λ1<k\lambda_{1}<k, increase λ1\lambda_{1} by 11.

  4. (2d)

    If r=0r=0 and λ1=k\lambda_{1}=k, replace one part kk by the parts k−5,2,2,2k-5,2,2,2.

Here ν∪2j\nu\cup 2^{j} means that jj parts equal to 22 are added. In each case the parts of ι⁡(λ)\iota(\lambda) lie in {2,…,k}\{2,\dots,k\} (we use 5≤k5\leq k and k−5≥4k-5\geq 4), and |ι⁡(λ)|=|λ|+1|\iota(\lambda)|=|\lambda|+1, since 3​r+1=2⋅3​r+12=5+2⋅3​r−423r+1=2\cdot\frac{3r+1}{2}=5+2\cdot\frac{3r-4}{2} and k+1=(k−5)+6k+1=(k-5)+6.

Let μ=ι⁡(λ)\mu=\iota(\lambda), and let jj be the number of parts 22 of μ\mu. In case (1), μ\mu has a part 33; in all other cases it has none. In case (2a), j=(3​r+1)/2≡2(mod3)j=(3r+1)/2\equiv 2\pmod{3}; in case (2b), j=(3​r−4)/2≡1(mod3)j=(3r-4)/2\equiv 1\pmod{3}; in case (2c), j=0j=0; and in case (2d), j=3j=3. Hence the five cases have pairwise disjoint images. Each case is injective: in case (1) we recover λ\lambda by replacing a part 33 of μ\mu by 22; in cases (2a) and (2b), rr is determined by jj, and ν\nu is obtained by deleting all parts 22 (and, in case (2b), one part 55); in case (2c), the largest part of μ\mu is strictly larger than all other parts and we decrease it by 11; in case (2d), we delete three parts 22 and one part k−5k-5 and insert a part kk. Thus ι\iota is injective and hk​(n)≥hk​(n−1)h_{k}(n)\geq h_{k}(n-1).

Now let n≥8n\geq 8. Every integer N≥6N\geq 6 is a sum of elements of {4,6,7,8,9}\{4,6,7,8,9\}: this holds for 6≤N≤96\leq N\leq 9, and for N≥10N\geq 10 it follows by induction using N=(N−4)+4N=(N-4)+4. Let ρ\rho be such a partition of n−2n-2, and let μ=ρ∪2\mu=\rho\cup 2. Then μ∈𝒫⁡(n)\mu\in\mathcal{P}(n), μ\mu has no part 33, exactly one part 22 (so j=1j=1) and no part 55. By the above description of the images, μ\mu is not in the image of ι\iota (it could only come from case (2b), whose images contain a part 55). Hence hk​(n)>hk​(n−1)h_{k}(n)>h_{k}(n-1). ∎

A direct computation shows that hk​(n)≥hk​(n−1)h_{k}(n)\geq h_{k}(n-1) for k∈{5,7,8}k\in\{5,7,8\} and 2≤n≤4002\leq n\leq 400. Within this range, the strict inequality hk​(n)>hk​(n−1)h_{k}(n)>h_{k}(n-1) for every n≥8n\geq 8 holds for k=7k=7, but fails for k=5k=5 at n=9,11,13n=9,11,13 and for k=8k=8 at n=9n=9.

Theorem 3.3 (the unboxed conjecture).

Let m≥9m\geq 9, and let a≠ba\neq b be integers with a,b≥7a,b\geq 7. Then the power series

Ea,b,m​(q)=(1−q)2(1−qa)​(1−qb)​(q,q)mE_{a,b,m}(q)=\frac{(1-q)^{2}}{(1-q^{a})(1-q^{b})\,(q;q)_{m}}

has constant term 11, coefficient −1-1 at q1q^{1}, and non-negative coefficients at qtq^{t} for all t≥2t\geq 2.

Proof.

Write 1/((1−qa)​(1−qb))=∑n≥0N⁡(n)​qn1/((1-q^{a})(1-q^{b}))=\sum_{n\geq 0}N(n)q^{n}, where N⁡(n)N(n) is the number of pairs (i,j)∈ℕ2(i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2} with i​a+j​b=nia+jb=n. By (1) with k=mk=m,

[qt]​Ea,b,m=∑n=0tN⁡(n)​dm​(t−n).[q^{t}]E_{a,b,m}=\sum_{n=0}^{t}N(n)\,d_{m}(t-n).

For t≤1t\leq 1 this gives 11 and −1-1. Let t≥2t\geq 2. By Lemma 3.2, the only possibly negative term is the one with t−n=1t-n=1, which equals −N⁡(t−1)-N(t-1). Since a+1≥8a+1\geq 8 and b+1≥8b+1\geq 8, the terms with n=t−1−an=t-1-a and n=t−1−bn=t-1-b (two distinct indices) are at least N⁡(t−1−a)N(t-1-a) and N⁡(t−1−b)N(t-1-b), respectively. Every representation t−1=i​a+j​bt-1=ia+jb has (i,j)≠(0,0)(i,j)\neq(0,0), because t−1≥1t-1\geq 1. If i≥1i\geq 1 it yields the representation (i−1,j)(i-1,j) of t−1−at-1-a, and otherwise j≥1j\geq 1 and it yields the representation (i,j−1)(i,j-1) of t−1−bt-1-b. This map is injective, so N⁡(t−1)≤N⁡(t−1−a)+N⁡(t−1−b)N(t-1)\leq N(t-1-a)+N(t-1-b). Hence [qt]​Ea,b,m≥0[q^{t}]E_{a,b,m}\geq 0. ∎

Theorem 3.3 is the limiting case N→∞N\to\infty of the Guo–Krattenthaler phenomenon. Indeed, [Nm]q→1/(q,q)m\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{N}{m}_{q}\to 1/(q;q)_{m} coefficientwise as N→∞N\to\infty, so

(1−q)2(1−qa)​(1−qb)​[Nm]q⟶Ea,b,m​(q).\frac{(1-q)^{2}}{(1-q^{a})(1-q^{b})}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{N}{m}_{q}\longrightarrow E_{a,b,m}(q).

In our situation the box has width 5​m5m, and the limit is already reached in the first 5​m+15m+1 coefficients.

Corollary 3.4.

Let m≥9m\geq 9 with m≢2,3(mod5)m\not\equiv 2,3\pmod{5}. Then [qt]​P(m)=[qt]​E2​m−1,3​m−1,m[q^{t}]P^{(m)}=[q^{t}]E_{2m-1,3m-1,m}, and this coefficient is non-negative, for 2≤t≤5​m2\leq t\leq 5m. By reciprocity, [qt]​P(m)≥0[q^{t}]P^{(m)}\geq 0 also for Dm−5​m≤t≤Dm−2D_{m}-5m\leq t\leq D_{m}-2.

Proof.

We have [6​mm]q=∏j=1m(1−q5​m+j)/(q,q)m≡1/(q,q)m(modq5​m+1)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{6m}{m}_{q}=\prod_{j=1}^{m}(1-q^{5m+j})/(q;q)_{m}\equiv 1/(q;q)_{m}\pmod{q^{5m+1}}. Multiplying by (1−q)2/((1−q2​m−1)​(1−q3​m−1))(1-q)^{2}/((1-q^{2m-1})(1-q^{3m-1})) gives P(m)≡E2​m−1,3​m−1,m(modq5​m+1)P^{(m)}\equiv E_{2m-1,3m-1,m}\pmod{q^{5m+1}}. Now apply Theorem 3.3 with a=2​m−1≥17a=2m-1\geq 17 and b=3​m−1b=3m-1. ∎

Remark 3.5.

Corollary 3.4 also explains the two exceptional values m=4m=4 and m=6m=6 in Theorem 4.3. Remark 3.6.

The naive approach would require the coefficient sequence of [6​mm]q\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{6m}{m}_{q} to be convex on the whole range [2,Dm/2][2,D_{m}/2]. This is false. For example, for m=10m=10 the second difference first becomes negative at t=199t=199, while D10/2=227D_{10}/2=227; asymptotically the inflection point of the Gaussian coefficients lies at distance of order m3/2m^{3/2} from the centre, whereas Dm/2D_{m}/2 is at distance of order mm. The reduction below avoids convexity and uses only a monotonicity property after one division.

4. Andrews’ lemma with one defect, and a reduction

The following lemma is an analogue of [4, Lemma 5.1], in which the unimodal input polynomial is allowed to have one “dip” at q1q^{1}.

5. An explicit bound: the conjecture holds for n≥2⋅1029n\geq 2\cdot 10^{29}

In this section we prove that Conjecture 4.4, and hence Conjecture 1.1, holds for all parameters beyond an explicit threshold. Unlike Section 4, we analyse P(m)P^{(m)} directly and do not go through UmU_{m}. The reason is that the coefficients of P(m)P^{(m)} involve no cancellation at leading order. The factor (1−q)2/((1−qa)​(1−qb))(1-q)^{2}/((1-q^{a})(1-q^{b})) is smooth near the relevant saddle point, so [qt]​P(m)[q^{t}]P^{(m)} is a positive multiple of a local central limit probability, up to a controlled error. 6. Graph binomial coefficients and qq-binomial coefficients

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a labelled graph with nn vertices. In [3], the number of kk-combinations of the unlabelled graph [G][G], i.e. the number of orbits of kk-subsets of VV under Aut⁡(G)\mathrm{Aut}(G), was denoted by (([G]k))\left(\!\!\binom{[G]}{k}\!\!\right) and called the graph binomial coefficient. By Burnside’s lemma [3, Theorem 2.1],

(([G]k))=1|Aut⁡(G)|​∑σ∈Aut⁡(G)|Vσk|,\left(\!\!\binom{[G]}{k}\!\!\right)=\frac{1}{|\mathrm{Aut}(G)|}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(G)}|V^{k}_{\sigma}|,

where VσkV^{k}_{\sigma} is the set of kk-subsets fixed by σ\sigma. Explicit formulas were obtained for the path PnP_{n} [3, Corollary 2.1] and for the directed cycle C→n\vec{C}_{n} [3, Corollary 2.2]:

(6) (([Pn]k))={12​(nk)n​ even,k​ odd,12​(nk)+12​(⌊n/2⌋⌊k/2⌋)otherwise,(([C→n]k))=1n​∑d|gcd⁡(n,k)φ⁡(d)​(n/dk/d).\left(\!\!\binom{[P_{n}]}{k}\!\!\right)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}\binom{n}{k}&n\text{ even},\ k\text{ odd},\\[2.0pt] \frac{1}{2}\binom{n}{k}+\frac{1}{2}\binom{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}\qquad\left(\!\!\binom{[\vec{C}_{n}]}{k}\!\!\right)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{d\mid\gcd(n,k)}\varphi(d)\binom{n/d}{k/d}.

The next proposition shows that these two graph binomial coefficients are hidden inside the Gaussian polynomial [nk]q\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{q}.

Proposition 6.1.

Let 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n. Then

(([Pn]k))=∑t≡0​(mod​ 2)[qt]​[nk]q,(([C→n]k))=∑t≡0​(mod​n)[qt]​[nk]q.\left(\!\!\binom{[P_{n}]}{k}\!\!\right)=\sum_{t\equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2)}[q^{t}]\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{q},\qquad\left(\!\!\binom{[\vec{C}_{n}]}{k}\!\!\right)=\sum_{t\equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ n)}[q^{t}]\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{q}.

For a polynomial ff and r≥1r\geq 1, the roots-of-unity filter gives

∑t≡0​(mod​r)[qt]​f=1r​∑j=0r−1f⁡(ωj),ω=e2​π​i/r.\sum_{t\equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ r)}[q^{t}]f=\frac{1}{r}\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}f(\omega^{j}),\qquad\omega=e^{2\pi i/r}.

Let ζ\zeta be a primitive dd-th root of unity with d|nd\mid n. Then

[nk]q=ζ={(n/dk/d)if ​d|k,0otherwise\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{q=\zeta}=\begin{cases}\binom{n/d}{k/d}&\text{if }d\mid k,\\ 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

(see, e.g., [6, Proposition 4.2]). For r=nr=n, grouping the jj’s according to the order dd of ωj\omega^{j} gives 1n​∑d|gcd⁡(n,k)φ⁡(d)​(n/dk/d)\frac{1}{n}\sum_{d\mid\gcd(n,k)}\varphi(d)\binom{n/d}{k/d}, which is the formula (6) for C→n\vec{C}_{n}. For r=2r=2 we get 12​((nk)+[nk]q=−1)\frac{1}{2}\big(\binom{n}{k}+\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{q=-1}\big). Moreover [nk]q=−1=(⌊n/2⌋⌊k/2⌋)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{q=-1}=\binom{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}, unless nn is even and kk is odd, in which case it is 00 (this is the case d=2d=2 of the evaluation above when nn is even; for nn odd it follows from [nk]q=[n−1k]q+qn−k​[n−1k−1]q\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{q}=\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}_{q}+q^{n-k}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k-1}_{q}). This gives (6) for PnP_{n}. ∎

Proposition 6.1 says that the Burnside averages of [3] for PnP_{n} and C→n\vec{C}_{n} are instances of the q=−1q=-1 phenomenon of Stembridge [7] and of the cyclic sieving phenomenon of Reiner, Stanton and White [6]. Combinatorially, the weight w⁡(S)=∑s∈Ss−(k2)w(S)=\sum_{s\in S}s-\binom{k}{2} on kk-subsets of {0,…,n−1}\{0,\dots,n-1\} is the bridge: a rotation of C→n\vec{C}_{n} by rr steps changes ww by r​krk modulo nn, and the reflection of PnP_{n} sends ww to k⁡(n−k)−wk(n-k)-w.

We now use this point of view for the polynomial P(m)P^{(m)}. Put a=2​m−1a=2m-1, b=3​m−1b=3m-1, c=m+2c=m+2, so that a+b+c=6​ma+b+c=6m, and consider the labelled graph

Γm=Pc⊔C→a⊔C→b\Gamma_{m}=P_{c}\ \sqcup\ \vec{C}_{a}\ \sqcup\ \vec{C}_{b}

whose vertices are labelled 0,1,…,6​m−10,1,\dots,6m-1 in this order: the path occupies {0,…,c−1}\{0,\dots,c-1\}, the first cycle {c,…,c+a−1}\{c,\dots,c+a-1\} and the second cycle the remaining bb labels. The group ℤa×ℤb\mathbb{Z}_{a}\times\mathbb{Z}_{b} of independent rotations of the two cycles is a subgroup of Aut⁡(Γm)\mathrm{Aut}(\Gamma_{m}). For an mm-subset SS of the vertices let

(l,i,j)=(|S∩Pc|,|S∩C→a|,|S∩C→b|).(l,i,j)=(|S\cap P_{c}|,\ |S\cap\vec{C}_{a}|,\ |S\cap\vec{C}_{b}|).

By the qq-Vandermonde convolution, applied twice,

(7) [6​mm]q=∑l+i+j=mqe⁡(l,i,j)​[cl]q​[ai]q​[bj]q,e⁡(l,i,j)=(c−l)​(i+j)+(a−i)​j,\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{6m}{m}_{q}=\sum_{l+i+j=m}q^{e(l,i,j)}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{c}{l}_{q}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{a}{i}_{q}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{b}{j}_{q},\qquad e(l,i,j)=(c-l)(i+j)+(a-i)j,

where the (l,i,j)(l,i,j)-term is the generating function, with respect to ww, of the mm-subsets SS of type (l,i,j)(l,i,j).

Call the type (l,i,j)(l,i,j) free if gcd⁡(i,a)=gcd⁡(j,b)=1\gcd(i,a)=\gcd(j,b)=1. If SS has free type, then no non-trivial rotation of C→a\vec{C}_{a} fixes S∩C→aS\cap\vec{C}_{a}: a subset of ℤa\mathbb{Z}_{a} fixed by a rotation of order d>1d>1 is a union of cycles of length dd, so d|id\mid i and d|ad\mid a. Similarly for C→b\vec{C}_{b}. Hence the ℤa×ℤb\mathbb{Z}_{a}\times\mathbb{Z}_{b}-orbit of SS has exactly a​bab elements.

Theorem 6.2.

Let m≥2m\geq 2 with m≢2,3(mod5)m\not\equiv 2,3\pmod{5}, and define

F(m)​(q)=∑l+i+j=mgcd⁡(i,a)=gcd⁡(j,b)=1qe⁡(l,i,j)​[cl]q⋅1[a]q​[ai]q⋅1[b]q​[bj]q,E(m)=P(m)−F(m).F^{(m)}(q)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l+i+j=m\\ \gcd(i,a)=\gcd(j,b)=1\end{subarray}}q^{e(l,i,j)}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{c}{l}_{q}\cdot\frac{1}{[a]_{q}}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{a}{i}_{q}\cdot\frac{1}{[b]_{q}}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{b}{j}_{q},\qquad E^{(m)}=P^{(m)}-F^{(m)}.

Then:

  1. (1)

    F(m)​(q)F^{(m)}(q) is a polynomial with non-negative integer coefficients, and F(m)​(1)F^{(m)}(1) is the number of ℤa×ℤb\mathbb{Z}_{a}\times\mathbb{Z}_{b}-orbits of mm-combinations of Γm\Gamma_{m} of free type;

  2. (2)

    E(m)​(q)E^{(m)}(q) is a polynomial, and

    [a]q​[b]q​E(m)​(q)=∑l+i+j=mgcd⁡(i,a)>1​ or ​gcd⁡(j,b)>1qe⁡(l,i,j)​[cl]q​[ai]q​[bj]q;[a]_{q}[b]_{q}\,E^{(m)}(q)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l+i+j=m\\ \gcd(i,a)>1\text{ or }\gcd(j,b)>1\end{subarray}}q^{e(l,i,j)}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{c}{l}_{q}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{a}{i}_{q}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{b}{j}_{q};
  3. (3)

    consequently, Conjecture 4.4 for mm is implied by the statement that E(m)​(q)+q+qDm−1E^{(m)}(q)+q+q^{D_{m}-1} has non-negative coefficients.

Proof.

(1) If gcd⁡(i,a)=1\gcd(i,a)=1 then gcd⁡(i,a−i)=1\gcd(i,a-i)=1, and by [4, Lemma 5.2] the quotient 1−q1−qa​[ai]q=1[a]q​[ai]q\frac{1-q}{1-q^{a}}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{a}{i}_{q}=\frac{1}{[a]_{q}}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{a}{i}_{q} is a polynomial with non-negative coefficients (it is the rational qq-Catalan number of type (i,a−i)(i,a-i)). The same holds for b,jb,j. Hence each summand of F(m)F^{(m)} is in ℕ⁡[q]\mathbb{N}[q]. At q=1q=1 each summand equals (cl)​(ai)​(bj)/(a​b)\binom{c}{l}\binom{a}{i}\binom{b}{j}/(ab), which is the number of free-type subsets of type (l,i,j)(l,i,j) divided by the common orbit size a​bab.

(2) This follows from (7), Proposition 2.1 and part (1), since E(m)E^{(m)} is the difference of two polynomials.

(3) This is immediate from P(m)=F(m)+E(m)P^{(m)}=F^{(m)}+E^{(m)} and F(m)≥0F^{(m)}\geq 0. ∎

Thus the free orbits, which form the “generic” part of the Burnside count for Γm\Gamma_{m}, contribute only non-negative coefficients. All possible negativity is concentrated in the mm-combinations whose intersection with one of the two cycles has a size sharing a factor with the length of that cycle. In particular, this includes the combinations that avoid one of the cycles completely, which are fixed by all rotations of that cycle. When aa and bb are both prime (for example m=10,16m=10,16), these are exactly the combinations with i=0i=0 or j=0j=0.

Proposition 6.3.

For every m∈{9,10,11,14,15,16,19,20,21,24,25,26,29,30}m\in\{9,10,11,14,15,16,19,20,21,24,25,26,29,30\}, the polynomial E(m)E^{(m)} has exactly two negative coefficients, namely −1-1 at q1q^{1} and at qDm−1q^{D_{m}-1}.

Proof.

Direct computation, as in Theorem 4.3. ∎

When aa and bb are both prime (m=10,16,24,30m=10,16,24,30 in Table 1), the free part dominates. When aa or bb has small prime factors, more types fail to be free and E(m)E^{(m)} becomes comparable to F(m)F^{(m)} (for example m=25m=25, where a=49a=49 and b=74b=74).

Remark 6.4.

A finer decomposition uses all free orbits, not only those of free type. By Möbius inversion, [ai]q=∑d|gcd⁡(a,i)Fra/d,i/d​(qd)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{a}{i}_{q}=\sum_{d\mid\gcd(a,i)}\mathrm{Fr}_{a/d,i/d}(q^{d}), where

Fra,i​(q)=∑d|gcd⁡(a,i)μ⁡(d)​[a/di/d]qd\mathrm{Fr}_{a,i}(q)=\sum_{d\mid\gcd(a,i)}\mu(d)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{a/d}{i/d}_{q^{d}}

is a qq-analogue of the number of aperiodic ii-subsets of ℤa\mathbb{Z}_{a}. We checked that Frn,i​(q)/[n]q∈ℕ⁡[q]\mathrm{Fr}_{n,i}(q)/[n]_{q}\in\mathbb{N}[q] for all 1≤i<n≤301\leq i<n\leq 30. Replacing [ai]q\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{a}{i}_{q} and [bj]q\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{b}{j}_{q} by Fra,i\mathrm{Fr}_{a,i} and Frb,j\mathrm{Fr}_{b,j} in F(m)F^{(m)} gives a non-negative part whose complement is very small. For instance, the ratio of the complement to P(m)​(1)P^{(m)}(1) is about 1.6%1.6\%, 0.17%0.17\% and 0.02%0.02\% for m=10,15,20m=10,15,20, and this complement again has exactly the two coefficients −1-1 for m∈{9,10,11,14,15,16,19,20}m\in\{9,10,11,14,15,16,19,20\}. It would be interesting to prove that Frn,i​(q)/[n]q∈ℕ⁡[q]\mathrm{Fr}_{n,i}(q)/[n]_{q}\in\mathbb{N}[q] in general and to give it a combinatorial interpretation.

7. Concluding remarks

The phenomenon described in Conjecture 4.4 does not seem to be special to the parameters (6​m,m,2​m−1,3​m−1)(6m,m,2m-1,3m-1). A computer search over all N≤45N\leq 45 shows that, among the 10 05310\,053 quotients [Nk]q/([a]q​[b]q)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{N}{k}_{q}/([a]_{q}[b]_{q}) with 2≤k≤N/22\leq k\leq N/2 and 2≤a≤b≤N2\leq a\leq b\leq N that are polynomials, 8 5828\,582 have exactly the two coefficients −1-1 at q1q^{1} and at qD−1q^{D-1} and no other negative coefficient. The exceptions occur mainly when aa is small compared with kk; in that case the coefficient −1-1 of q1q^{1} is propagated to q1+a,q1+2​a,…q^{1+a},q^{1+2a},\dots and is not compensated. For instance, for the families

1[2​m−1]q​[6​m−1]q​[12​mm]q,1[4​m−1]q​[6​m−1]q​[12​m5​m]q,1[4​m−1]q​[6​m−1]q​[12​m3​m]q,\frac{1}{[2m-1]_{q}[6m-1]_{q}}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{12m}{m}_{q},\qquad\frac{1}{[4m-1]_{q}[6m-1]_{q}}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{12m}{5m}_{q},\qquad\frac{1}{[4m-1]_{q}[6m-1]_{q}}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{12m}{3m}_{q},

every case with 2≤m≤102\leq m\leq 10 in which the quotient is a polynomial shows exactly the Guo–Krattenthaler pattern. Lemma 4.1 applies verbatim to such quotients.

The most pressing open point is the finite gap left by Theorem 5.1.

Problem 7.1.

Lower the threshold 103010^{30} of Theorem 5.1 far enough to meet the range m≤300m\leq 300 covered by Theorem 4.3. The threshold is driven by regime (I) of Section 5, i.e. by tt just above 5​m5m, where the effective number of active Bernoulli variables is only of order t\sqrt{t}, and by the crude constants of Lemma 5.5. Corollary 3.4 disposes of the range t≤5​mt\leq 5m by a purely combinatorial argument. Extending it to t≤ε​m2t\leq\varepsilon m^{2} would mean controlling the “box corrections” ∏j=1m(1−q5​m+j)\prod_{j=1}^{m}(1-q^{5m+j}) in [6​mm]q=∏j=1m(1−q5​m+j)/(q,q)m\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{6m}{m}_{q}=\prod_{j=1}^{m}(1-q^{5m+j})/(q;q)_{m}. Such an extension would leave only the moderate- and central-deviation ranges to the analytic argument, where the effective number of variables is of order mm.

Problem 7.2.

Characterize the quadruples (N,k,a,b)(N,k,a,b) for which [Nk]q/([a]q​[b]q)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{N}{k}_{q}/([a]_{q}[b]_{q}) is a polynomial whose only negative coefficients are −1-1 at q1q^{1} and at qD−1q^{D-1}. In particular, is this always the case when [Nk]q/[a]q\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{N}{k}_{q}/[a]_{q} is weakly increasing from q1q^{1} to its middle coefficient?

By Lemma 4.1, the answer to the last question is affirmative as soon as, in addition, the coefficients of qbq^{b} and qb+1q^{b+1} in [Nk]q/[a]q\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{N}{k}_{q}/[a]_{q} are distinct.
